abdicate.meaning: To give up a position of power, such as the place of a king.

seclusion.meaning: A state of being kept away from other people.

brooded.meaning: Sat over something with worry, as a bird sits on eggs.

precincts.meaning: The area around a place, especially a place that is special.

fender.meaning: A low metal guard in front of a fire, to stop pieces of wood falling out.

incumbrances.meaning: Things, such as children, that make life harder and take time and money.

delinquencies.meaning: Small wrong things done, such as not doing one's duty.

perjured.meaning: Having broken a promise that was made to God.

ignominiously.meaning: In a way that brings great loss of respect.

practicability.meaning: The fact that something can really be done and works.

millinery.meaning: Women's things worn on the head, and the making of them.

harangue.meaning: A long, loud speech that tries to make people listen.

paragraphs.context: In France the young girls have a dull time of it till they are married
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer says that in France girls are free after marriage, but in America young wives are put on the shelf.
paragraphs.simple: In France young girls have a dull time until they are married, and then 'Long live liberty' becomes their motto. In America, as everyone knows, girls sign the declaration of independence early and enjoy their freedom with republican spirit. But young wives usually give up their power when the first heir comes, and go into a life almost as shut away as a French nunnery, though not as quiet. Whether they like it or not, they are as good as put on the shelf as soon as the wedding excitement is over. Most could say, as a very pretty woman did the other day, 'I am as handsome as ever, but no one notices me because I am married.'

paragraphs.context: The poor man was very uncomfortable, for the children had bereft him of his wife
paragraphs.mainIdea: John feels shut out from home, so after six months he starts to spend evenings at the Scotts'.
paragraphs.simple: The poor man was very uncomfortable, because the children had taken his wife from him. Home was only a nursery. The endless 'hushing' made him feel like a rough stranger whenever he went into the holy area of Babyland. He bore it patiently for six months. When nothing got better, he did what other fathers in his state do and tried to find a little comfort elsewhere. Scott had married and set up house not far away. John got into the habit of running over for an hour or two in the evening when his own parlor was empty and his own wife was singing lullabies that never seemed to end. Mrs. Scott was a lively, pretty girl with nothing to do but be pleasant, and she did it very well. Her parlor was always bright and nice, with the chessboard ready, the piano in tune, plenty of gay gossip and a nice little supper set out in a tempting way.

sentences.context: if John goes on so much longer I might as well be widowed
sentences.simple: If John goes on like this much longer, it would be the same as being a widow.
sentences.grammar: 'If John goes on ... I might as well be' mixes a real 'if' with 'might as well', which says that two choices are equal. 'Widowed' means with a dead husband.

sentences.context: as if he felt that justice was tempered with mercy
sentences.simple: It was as if Demi felt that fair punishment can come together with kindness.
sentences.grammar: 'As if' introduces something that only seems true. 'Tempered with' means 'made softer by'. The verb phrase is in the passive: 'justice was tempered'.

come to the rescue.meaning: To come and help someone who is in trouble.
